title: THE INTERPLAY OF PSYCHOLOGY, PHYSIOLOGY AND ARCHITECTURAL DESIGN: AN OVERVIEW
review_question: To create a better understanding of how the complex relationship between architectural design and human psychology and physiology evolved and its implications in today's world, by exploring brain structure/function, evolutionary benefits, modern societal impacts, and the importance of nature in the built environment.

findings.antecedent: Objects and places that increased chances for survival (evolutionary context)
findings.quote: Evolutionarily, human brains have been encoded to associate a sense of pleasure with objects and places that increased our chances for survival

findings.antecedent: Characteristics of the savanna (advantageously spaced trees, lush countryside, water, food)
findings.quote: the Savanna Hypothesis suggests the characteristics of the savanna are encoded in our brains...thus influencing our preferences

findings.antecedent: Chronic stress
findings.consequent: Detrimental mental and physical health issues (anxiety, insomnia, depression, weakened immune system, muscle pain, heart disease, high blood pressure)
findings.quote: Constant or chronic stress can lead to extremely detrimental, and even permanent, mental and physical health issues.

findings.antecedent: Prolonged stress (cortisol production)
findings.consequent: Shortened telomeres, premature cell death, accelerated aging
findings.quote: prolonged stress physically shortens the parts of chromosomes known as telomeres... resulting in premature cell death and acceleration of the aging process

findings.antecedent: Perception of beautiful design
findings.consequent: Sense of pleasure, release of oxytocin, endorphins, DHEA
findings.quote: Seeing something we define as beautiful causes us to feel a sense of pleasure; physiologically this results from the release of oxytocin, endorphins and DHEA

findings.antecedent: Architectural elements with patterns similar to survival-beneficial locations (evolutionary basis)
findings.quote: Buildings that provide us with a sense of pleasure are those that incorporate the architectural elements our brain recognizes as having similar characteristics or patterns to locations that helped our ancestors survive.

findings.antecedent: Similar advantageous patterns in built environment
findings.quote: Seeing similar advantageous patterns in our built environment today evokes a similar physiological reaction.

findings.antecedent: Chaos or unpredictability (lack of organized pattern)
findings.quote: chaos or unpredictability, the opposite of organized pattern, can negatively impact us physiologically.

findings.antecedent: Information exceeding cognitive limit (7 components)
findings.quote: Our human “cognitive limit” is 7 components... after that it becomes stressful for our brain to try and remember more.

findings.antecedent: Like object grouping (patterns, symmetry)
findings.consequent: Avoidance of cognitive overload, easier scene reading
findings.quote: Such ‘like object grouping' to avoid cognitive overload, employed in nature and used by humans as a survival tactic, is also applicable to the built environment.

findings.antecedent: Environments devoid of information (lack patterns, symmetries)
findings.consequent: Cognitive boredom, stress response (similar to perceived danger), active repulsion
findings.quote: environments devoid of information to process... buildings that lack patterns and symmetries either don't register or actively repel us... cognitive boredom can induce the same stress response as perceived danger.

findings.antecedent: Buildings incorporating Alexander's 15 fundamental properties (including scaling symmetry)
findings.quote: Alexander proposed that successful buildings are those perceived by humans to have “life”, which he defines by his 15 fundamental properties

findings.antecedent: Buildings incorporating symmetries, patterns, fundamental properties (mimicking nature)
findings.consequent: Perceived as beautiful, sense of safety, security, well-being, survival, pleasure, release of oxytocin/endorphins/DHEA, reduced sympathetic nervous system activity, restoration of body/immune system/telomeres, beneficial mental/physical health
findings.quote: buildings that incorporate these symmetries, patterns and fundamental properties to be more beautiful because our brains have been physiologically conditioned by evolution to associate those patterns with safety, security, well-being and survival.

findings.antecedent: Architectural design mimicking forest (tree-like pillars, branching canopies) (e.g., La Sagrada Familia)
findings.quote: Gaudí's inspiration for the cathedral came from the forest. Walking into the cathedral, one is greeted by hundreds of 78-foot-tall pillars that branch off at the top and converge into the ceiling and one another, like the intertwining branches of tree canopies

findings.antecedent: Architectural design mimicking natural forms (bubbles), transparent domes coexisting with nature (e.g., Eden Project)
findings.quote: The architect Nicholas Grimshaw found his inspiration in bubbles, making it easy for the translucent domes to effortlessly coexist with the natural surroundings

findings.antecedent: 3x3 grid pattern (symmetry, scaling hierarchy)
findings.consequent: Easier scene reading, prevention of stress-inducing information overload
findings.quote: symmetry of like objects allows for the brain to categorize these like objects... thus making the scene easier to read, preventing stress-inducing information overload

findings.antecedent: 3x3 grid pattern (similarity to human face structure)
findings.consequent: Popularity and importance of the pattern (due to evolutionary facial recognition mechanisms)
findings.quote: The popularity and importance of the 3 x 3 grid pattern can be understood based on the similarity of the pattern to the structure of the human face.

findings.antecedent: Inverted facial patterns (vs. upright)
findings.quote: humans are less accurate at recognizing faces when the pattern is inverted as opposed to upright... due to our “face recognition cells” analyzing bilateral symmetry on a vertical axis.

findings.antecedent: Upright 'T' shape (vaguely resembling facial structure/3x3 grid)
findings.quote: the infants were partial to the shapes when they were right side up and most resembled faces

findings.antecedent: Architectural forms/patterns resembling 3x3 grid/human face
findings.consequent: Stimulation of physiological reactions (similar to infant preference for faces)
findings.quote: The close resemblance of the 3 x 3 grid pattern to the human face raises the distinct possibility that humans subconsciously see faces in certain architectural forms and patterns, stimulating the same physiological reactions

findings.antecedent: Poorly designed architecture (absence of natural geometries, structural imbalance)
findings.consequent: Negative psychological impact (anxiety, illness), negative physiological impact
findings.quote: “Our bodies signal the absence of natural geometries and structural balance with anxiety and illness”

findings.antecedent: Monotonously repetitive, unstimulating, 'box' design (post-WWII housing)
findings.quote: small, unstimulating houses (i.e., they lacked characteristics that activate our pleasure response) in the 1950's with a monotonously repetitive one floor ‘box' design

findings.antecedent: Monochromatic colors, poorly placed windows, absence of architectural detail, repetitive styles (Modernism aesthetic)
findings.consequent: Sensory deprivation, lack of intellectual stimulation, cold/unwelcoming environment, lack of physiological/psychological well-being
findings.quote: Monochromatic colors, poorly placed windows, an absence of architectural detail, and repetitive styles produced a unique form of sensory deprivation. Not only did this trend result in a lack of intellectual stimulation, it also effectively removed the positive aspects of human touch, creating a cold, unwelcoming environment that lacked the ability to produce a physiological or psychological a sense of well-being.

findings.antecedent: Battered houses, abandoned/dilapidated buildings
findings.quote: battered houses and neighborhoods with abandoned and dilapidated buildings make us feel unsafe and evoke a sense of fear and anxiety
key_citations: Could bad buildings damage your mental health?, 2016

findings.antecedent: Built environment with variety of independent shops and unique spaces
findings.quote: humans are generally healthier when their built environment contains a variety of independent shops and unique spaces rather than cement buildings and repetitive chain stores

findings.antecedent: Large, generic building (vs. unique, lively restaurants with open doors/windows)
findings.quote: the former environment resulted in the lowest arousal level of the study, while the latter produced a high level of excitement

findings.antecedent: Small amounts of boredom
findings.quote: even small amounts of boredom can actually induce stress

findings.antecedent: Lack of novelty or change in urban design
findings.quote: “The holy grail in urban design is to produce some kind of novelty or change every few seconds, otherwise, we become cognitively disengaged"

findings.antecedent: Poorly maintained buildings/spaces OR dull repetitive buildings
findings.consequent: Nervousness, fear, boredom, physiologic stress response
findings.quote: Poorly maintained buildings and spaces make us nervous and fearful, while dull repetitive buildings bore us; both cause a physiologic stress response.

findings.antecedent: Contact with nature
findings.quote: Wilson proposed that this necessity was a vestige of the attraction experienced by our human ancestors for all living things; he also felt that we possessed a genetic predisposition to that attraction

findings.antecedent: Architecture/designs incorporating elements of nature
findings.quote: This ingrained affinity for the natural environment and living things helps to explain, at least in part, our preference for architecture and designs that incorporate elements of nature

findings.antecedent: Proximity/visual connection with plants/animals/people OR built environments mimicking nature via symmetries/patterns
findings.quote: These positive effects from biophilia are made possible by two distinct factors: a) proximity and visual connection with plants, animals and people; and b) built environments that successfully mimic that natural environment through proper symmetries and patterns

findings.antecedent: Too much nature
findings.consequent: Stress-type response (similar to too much uniformity in buildings)
findings.quote: too much nature can evoke a similar stress-type response seen with too much uniformity in buildings.

findings.antecedent: Arousing but unpleasant environment
findings.consequent: Panicked, tense, sympathetic nervous system activation
findings.quote: When an environment is arousing but unpleasant, we feel panicked and tense, and our sympathetic nervous system is activated.

findings.antecedent: Pleasant environment (arousing)
findings.quote: When environments are pleasant, they can either be arousing (making us feel excited and stimulated, causing chemicals like oxytocin to be released)

findings.antecedent: Pleasant environment (not arousing)
findings.consequent: Pleasantly relaxed, at peace, smooth autonomic nervous system function
findings.quote: they can be not arousing (making us feel pleasantly relaxed and at peace, helping our autonomic nervous system to run smoothly).

findings.antecedent: Environment too extreme on arousal spectrum (too high or too low)
findings.consequent: Uncomfortable feeling, physiological response, seeking arousal reduction/sensory enhancement
findings.quote: being too extreme on either side causes us to feel uncomfortable which generates a physiological response that causes us to seek either arousal reduction or sensory enhancement.

findings.antecedent: Environments providing ample amounts of information to process
findings.quote: we prefer environments that provide us with ample amounts of information to process

findings.antecedent: Simplistic/unimaginative designs (post-WWII) vs. ornate/classical architecture
findings.quote: simplistic and unimaginative designs of the immediate post-WWII era haven't lasted, while more ornate architecture using more classical columns, colonnades and entablature has lasted across millennia.

findings.antecedent: Too much non-reducible information
findings.quote: too much non-reducible information tends to push the arousing environment away from pleasant and closer to unpleasant

findings.antecedent: Environmental components (coherence, legibility, complexity, mystery)
findings.quote: The categories defined in the model (coherence, legibility, complexity and mystery), are believed by Kaplan to increase an individual's preference for a specific environment.

findings.antecedent: Good architectural design (symmetries, patterns of nature, visual similarities to nature, patterns for smooth information processing)
findings.quote: The stress reducing capabilities of those designs are a direct result of our brain recognizing visual similarities to nature and to patterns that allow smooth information processing

findings.antecedent: Contact with nature/restorative environments
findings.quote: Merely being in contact with nature and these environments is enough to set this process in motion.

findings.antecedent: Viewing pictures of nature
findings.quote: simply viewing pictures of nature had the ability to lessen the effects of exam induced stress

findings.antecedent: Hospital room with window overlooking nature (vs. brick wall)
findings.quote: Ulrich demonstrated shortened post-surgical recovery times for patients in hospital rooms with a window overlooking a small stand of trees compared to patients recovering in a room with a brick wall

findings.antecedent: Exposure to nature video (vs. urban scenes)
findings.consequent: Increased positive feelings, lower blood pressure, muscle tension, skin conductance levels
findings.quote: The participants exposed to the nature video experienced an increase in positive feelings and were found to have lower blood pressure, muscle tension, and skin conductance levels; the urban scenes failed to produce any of these positive physiologic effects

findings.antecedent: Personal shelter as natural environment (refuge and prospect)
findings.quote: Turning our personal shelter into a natural environmental provides us with refuge (a safe sheltered place) and prospect (an unobstructed view of the surrounding environment)

findings.antecedent: Windows with a view of nature OR pictures of nature
findings.consequent: Restorative effects (similar to direct nature contact)
findings.quote: having windows with a view of nature is easily done. When this can't be done... simply adding pictures of nature to one's house can produce similar effects.

findings.antecedent: Large windows/glass walls with unobstructed nature view OR indoor plants
findings.quote: houses that have large windows or glass walls permitting an unobstructed view of nature... or that have the space to place plants inside, will be the most beneficial at producing the desired psychological benefits.

findings.antecedent: Adaptation of natural landscapes into built environment
findings.quote: Adaption of such natural landscapes into our built environment is also an essential part of developing an attachment... to that space

findings.antecedent: Bland/featureless urban architecture OR urban areas devoid of natural elements
findings.consequent: Low-level stress, insufficient mental stimulation, elimination of restorative benefits
findings.quote: Urban architecture is often bland and featureless which we now know creates low level stress and results in insufficient mental stimulation. Urban areas are also frequently devoid of elements of the natural environment which not only creates further stress but also eliminates the potential for the important restorative benefits nature can provide.

synthesis_conclusions: Good architectural design has clear psychological and physiological benefits that extend beyond mere aesthetic appeal.
Poor architectural design and execution are directly linked to negative health and psychological issues.
There is a better understanding of the human evolutionary and physiological basis for many psychological responses to design.
Leveraging current knowledge and technological tools, architecture can be created to be not only aesthetically beautiful but also psychologically beneficial.

Given the increasing prevalence of health problems like chronic stress, employing architectural design that fails to incorporate elements known to produce psychological and restorative benefits is no longer an acceptable option.

The societal perception of architectural design as merely an art form, which strips it of its meaningful legitimacy, needs to be reconsidered to ensure the field receives the necessary resources to address the psychological impacts of thoughtless design and improve the built environment.
evidence_gaps: Lack of general public understanding and funding for architectural design's psychological and restorative impact, which prevents addressing thoughtless design and improving the built environment.

mechanism_chain.description: Evolutionary mechanism linking environmental features to human affective responses.
